<reason>A built a tighter, more coherent path: fines target only documented repeat refusal, "meaningful" implies proportionality, and the willing self-select out via warnings/audits. Crucially, A's pressure question forced B to admit it had no tool for the well-resourced willful refuser, and B's Rebuttal 2 answer conceded "a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal" — a hybrid that functionally grants A's mechanism. B tried to walk this back in closing by insisting it accepted "a different policy," but that hedge came late and looked evasive after the concession was already on record. B's strongest surviving point — that A's own "overwhelming majority fail" statistic shows the target population is mostly capacity-poor, not willful, and that engaging with a warning doesn't manufacture capacity to fix vendor-locked systems — was raised well but never fully weaponized against A's self-selection claim, and A's closing simply reasserted self-selection without directly confronting the "good-faith-but-still-fails" scenario. On balance A answered more of the live pressure, converted a concession into a decisive closing frame, and left a cleaner reason to vote for the motion; B's case remained coherent but ended slightly on the back foot.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question forcing B to name a mechanism for the willful, well-resourced refuser, and B's subsequent Rebuttal 2 concession of "a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal" — which A then used in Closing to claim the debate was effectively over, and B could only partially contain in its own Closing.</best_rebuttal>
